name: wmbusmeters
desc: Read wired or wireless mbus protocol to acquire utility meter readings
why: Decodes wireless M-Bus utility meter telegrams from cheap radio dongles, letting you read your neighbourhood's water and power meters.

brief.what_it_is: wmbusmeters is an open-source program that reads utility meter readings from wired M-Bus or wireless wM-Bus (OMS-compatible) meters. It takes in raw telegrams from radio dongles (im871a, iu891a, amb8465/Metis, amb3665, cul, rc1180, or rtl-sdr software-radio sticks), from serial M-Bus master converters, or from files, pipes, stdin, or MQTT topics. It decodes them with meter drivers into key-value pairs and outputs them as human-readable text, CSV fields, or JSON, which can be published via MQTT, posted to a REST API, inserted into a database, or written to log and meter files. The README's example turns the hex telegram 1844AE4C4455223368077A55000000_041389E20100023B0000 into a line showing a water meter's id, total m3, flow and timestamp.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames the problem as getting utility meter readings out of wired or wireless M-Bus meters, and points out that a raw value like a 32-bit signed volume in storage slot 1 means nothing without knowing what it measures (last month's billing reading, last year's gas delivered, and so on). The drivers supply that meaning.
brief.how_it_works: Dongles or serial ports deliver telegrams to the program, which matches each one to a meter by id and selects a driver, either auto-detected or named in the config. Drivers translate manufacturer-specific bytes into named fields; since version 2.0 many drivers are written as declarative xmq/ixml text files rather than C++, and the README says new drivers should be written in that form. Users can also add calculated fields with formulas that track SI units, and run a shell command with METER_ environment variables for each reading.

commands_seen.context: Build from source and install as a daemon. The README says this only works on GNU/Linux; on macOS it suggests starting wmbusmetersd from a script instead.
Start the daemon after the config file at /etc/wmbusmeters.conf has been set up (device=auto:t1 in the example).
Run from the command line instead of the daemon, probing for any attached dongle and listening on T1 mode. The README says to use auto for testing and a full device path in production.
Listen for C1 telegrams on any available dongle, and decode meter 12345678 named MyTapWater with auto-detected driver and a 16-byte key.
Decode a single hex telegram given on the command line with no config. The README says it prints the id, manufacturer, and recommended driver (here lansenpu).
Run without config files, output JSON, and store the latest reading per meter in a directory. NOKEY is used for meters that do not encrypt their data.
Search the built-in list of meter drivers by keyword.
List the fields a given driver can output, for use with --selectfields.
Trigger a reload of the daemon's config files without restarting it.
Run in the terminal using the config files in /etc, for installs that cannot run as a daemon.

brief.install_notes: Distribution packages: dnf install wmbusmeters on Fedora 31 or newer, and a Debian package that is in Experimental. Docker and Snap images are marked experimental. Building from source is recommended by the README because development is fast: remove any wM-Bus dongle or rtl-sdr stick from the computer first, then run ./configure; make; sudo make install. Config lives in /etc/wmbusmeters.conf and /etc/wmbusmeters.d (or a directory passed with --useconfig). Each meter gets a file with name, id, key and driver. For rtl-sdr, the rtl_sdr and rtl_wmbus binaries must exist in /usr/bin or next to the wmbusmeters binary. Serial M-Bus needs a bus alias such as MAIN=/dev/ttyUSB0:mbus:2400. The wiki at wmbusmeters.github.io covers the snap and more.
brief.standout: Drivers are being moved out of C++ into a declarative xmq/ixml format that can be edited as text, and the maintainer says new drivers should be written that way and will not be accepted as C++. The project also gives an explicit upgrade promise: if a meter is pinned to a named driver, the JSON keys will not change incompatibly on upgrade, and the README spells out that rule.
brief.status: Maintained. The GitHub releases page shows 3.0.0 as latest, dated 2026-06-17, with 2.0.0 on 2026-03-01 and 1.20.0 on 2026-01-27, so releases are frequent. The README's usage text prints version 3.1.0, which is ahead of the latest tagged release, so the README may be slightly ahead of the tags. The README also says development progresses quickly.
brief.caveats: Runs on GNU/Linux, macOS, FreeBSD and Raspberry Pi. make install is GNU/Linux only. Hardware is required: a supported wM-Bus dongle, an rtl-sdr stick, or a serial M-Bus converter. The cul dongle is limited to shorter telegrams unless a firmware fix is applied. The rc1180 listens only to T1. Encrypted meters need that meter's own key, so this reads meters you have keys for, not arbitrary neighbours' meters. Plain /dev/ttyUSB0 no longer works and the device has to be named with its type. Auto-probing of serial ports is slow, and the README advises a full device path in production. Using a driver of auto in production is discouraged. Driver licensing is GPLv3 or later per the --license option; the README does not state a licence on the page I read. The README was truncated at 40000 characters, so later sections were not read.
quotes: The program acquires utility meter readings from wired m-bus or wireless wm-bus meters.
I am not accepting new drivers as C++ code.
So wmbusmeters strives to guarantee that if you have specified the driver name, then wmbusmeters can be safely upgraded at any time.

judge.reason: It turns obscure wireless utility-meter telegrams into meaningful readings, even from RTL-SDR, and its declarative drivers offer a door into vendor-specific protocol decoding.

entry.title: wmbusmeters
entry.tldr: Decodes wired and wireless M-Bus utility meter telegrams from radio dongles into readable fields, so you can read your own water or heat meter.
entry.deeper_look:
wmbusmeters takes raw telegrams from a radio dongle (im871a, iu891a, amb8465, cul, rc1180, or an rtl-sdr stick), a serial M-Bus converter, or a file, pipe, stdin or MQTT topic. It matches each telegram to a meter by id, picks a driver, and prints named fields as text, CSV or JSON. From there the readings can go to MQTT, a REST API, a database or plain files.

The interesting part is the drivers. A telegram is just bytes, and the README points out that a 32-bit signed volume in storage slot 1 means nothing until you know whether it is last month's billing reading or last year's gas delivered. The drivers supply that meaning. Its example turns the hex telegram `1844AE4C4455223368077A55000000_041389E20100023B0000` into a line with a water meter's id, total m3, flow and timestamp.

Since version 2.0 many drivers are declarative xmq/ixml text files rather than C++, and the maintainer says new drivers must be written that way. You can also add calculated fields using formulas that track SI units, or run a shell command with METER_ environment variables for each reading.

You can decode a single hex telegram from the command line with no hardware at all, which makes a decent first look at how these meters talk.
entry.install:
brew install wmbusmeters
# Real use needs hardware: a supported wM-Bus dongle, an rtl-sdr stick, or a serial M-Bus converter. For rtl-sdr, the rtl_sdr and rtl_wmbus binaries must be in /usr/bin or next to the wmbusmeters binary. The README recommends building from source (./configure; make; sudo make install, GNU/Linux only) because development moves fast.

try_this.what_happens: Decodes one hex telegram with no config or hardware, printing the meter id, manufacturer and recommended driver (lansenpu in the README's example).
Searches the built-in meter drivers by keyword.
Probes for any attached dongle and listens for T1-mode telegrams from meters in range.

entry.whats_unique: Meter drivers are moving to editable declarative text files instead of C++. The project also promises that if you pin a named driver, the JSON keys will not change incompatibly on upgrade.
entry.caveats: Real readings need a dongle, and encrypted meters need their own key, so this reads meters you have keys for, not arbitrary neighbours' meters.
